stats2data_application

Source: vignettes/stats2data_application.Rmd
stats2data_application.Rmd

Overview

stats2data simulates raw datasets whose summary statistics match reported summary statistics (the targets). Each module defines an objective, the discrepancy between the summary statistics of a candidate dataset and the targets, and minimizes it with simulated annealing. A run stops once the best objective value falls below the convergence threshold thresh or once the iteration budget is spent. In this vignette, a run whose best objective value is below thresh is called converged.

Convergence is a statement about the optimization only: the simulated summary statistics reproduce the targets to within thresh. Many different datasets share the same summary statistics, and a simulated dataset is one of them. The results below are therefore described in terms of the optimization (objective values, target-vs-simulated differences, run-to-run variability), not in terms of how closely the simulated data resemble the unobserved original data.

The vignette works through four examples:

  1. the Descriptives module (optim_vec()), using the reported marginal statistics of Bardwell et al. (2007);
  2. the MLR module (optim_mlr()), using the reported correlations and regression estimates of the same study;
  3. the ANOVA module (optim_aov()), using the reported cell means and F-statistics of Reynolds and Besner (2008), as in the accompanying manuscript;
  4. the parallel workflow (parallel_optim()), using the ANOVA example.

Across the examples, the following functions are demonstrated:

  • the optimization functions optim_vec(), optim_mlr(), optim_aov(), and parallel_optim();
  • the GRIM check check_grim();
  • the inspection methods print(), summary(), get_stats(), get_rmse(), and coef();
  • the plotting functions plot_convergence(), plot_cooling(), plot_fit(), plot_stability(), and the plot() methods;
  • the Shiny interface run_app().

Installation 

if (!requireNamespace("devtools", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("sebastian-lortz/stats2data")

Shiny interface

All three modules and the parallel workflow are also available in a point-and-click interface:

library(stats2data)
run_app()

The tabs Descriptives, ANOVA, and Linear Regression correspond to optim_vec(), optim_aov(), and optim_mlr(). The inputs of each tab correspond to the arguments of the function (the info icon of each input names the argument), and setting Number of Runs above one calls parallel_optim(). The results panel offers the plots and summaries shown in this vignette. The Download button exports the result object, the simulated data, and the R code of the function call, which reproduces the result in R.

Setup 

library(stats2data)
library(ggplot2)

1. Descriptives module: Bardwell et al. (2007)

Bardwell et al. (2007, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jad.2006.06.013) examined whether depressive symptoms or apnea severity better predict fatigue in patients with obstructive sleep apnea. The raw data are not publicly available. The study reports means and standard deviations of four variables for N = 60 patients, rounded to one decimal. optim_vec() simulates one vector per variable that reproduces its target mean and SD.

1.1 Encoding the targets 

N           <- 60
target_mean <- c(Apnea.1 = 48.8, Apnea.2 = 17.3, Depression = 12.6, Fatigue = 10.8)
target_sd   <- c(Apnea.1 = 27.1, Apnea.2 = 20.1, Depression = 11.3, Fatigue = 7.3)
integer     <- c(FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)
range       <- matrix(
  c( 15,    0,  0,  0,    # lower bounds
    111, 80.9, 49, 28),   # upper bounds
  nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE
)

Apnea.1 and Apnea.2 are treated as continuous, Depression and Fatigue as integer-valued sum scores. range holds one column of lower and upper bounds per variable.

1.2 GRIM check

For integer-valued data, not every mean is attainable: the sum of N integers divided by N can only take values on a grid of width 1 / N. The GRIM test (Brown & Heathers, 2017) checks whether a reported mean, rounded to decimals, lies on that grid:

check_grim(n = N, target_mean = target_mean[["Depression"]], decimals = 1)
#> $test
#> [1] TRUE
#> 
#> $grim_mean
#> [1] 12.6
check_grim(n = N, target_mean = target_mean[["Fatigue"]],    decimals = 1)
#> $test
#> [1] TRUE
#> 
#> $grim_mean
#> [1] 10.8

With N = 60 and one decimal, the grid width (1 / 60) is smaller than the rounding unit (0.1), so every mean passes. The check is informative for small samples or more decimals; for a mean that fails, grim_mean returns the nearest attainable mean (hypothetical values):

check_grim(n = 7, target_mean = 3.45, decimals = 2)
#> $test
#> [1] FALSE
#> 
#> $grim_mean
#> [1] 3.43

1.3 Running the optimizer

For continuous variables, optim_vec() starts from a vector whose mean lies within thresh of the target mean and anneals the values toward the target SD; the moves keep the mean fixed. For integer variables, it draws a distribution from SPRITE (Heathers et al., 2018) via rsprite2 whose mean and SD match the targets at the number of decimals given by sprite_prec. The objective of each variable is the absolute difference between its simulated and target SD.

Both statistics are reported to one decimal, so sprite_prec = c(1, 1), and thresh = 0.05 is set to half a unit of the last reported decimal. All other arguments are at their defaults (max_iter = 5e5, init_temp = 1e-3, cooling_rate = NULL, i.e. (max_iter - 10) / max_iter, max_starts = 3).

set.seed(2026)
result_vec <- optim_vec(
  N           = N,
  target_mean = target_mean,
  target_sd   = target_sd,
  range       = range,
  integer     = integer,
  sprite_prec = c(1, 1),
  thresh      = 0.05
)

1.4 Inspecting the result

print() shows the sample size and the best objective value per variable:

result_vec
#> stats2data Descriptives result
#>   Variables: 4 
#>   N:         60 
#>   Best objective per variable:
#>     Apnea.1: 0.04797
#>     Apnea.2: 0.04888
#>     Depression: 0.02264
#>     Fatigue: 0.04108

The best objective values are below thresh = 0.05 for all four variables. summary() adds the target and simulated means and SDs and their RMSEs; the largest absolute difference between a simulated and a target mean is 0.0497:

summary(result_vec)
#> stats2data Descriptives Summary
#> -----------------------------------------------
#> N: 60  | Variables: 4 
#> 
#> Best objective per variable:
#>   Apnea.1: 0.04797
#>   Apnea.2: 0.04888
#>   Depression: 0.02264
#>   Fatigue: 0.04108
#> 
#> RMSE
#>   Means: 0.03875 
#>   SDs:   0.0415 
#> 
#> Target vs. Simulated:
#>    variable target_mean sim_mean target_sd sim_sd
#>     Apnea.1        48.8    48.75      27.1 27.052
#>     Apnea.2        17.3    17.35      20.1 20.051
#>  Depression        12.6    12.63      11.3 11.323
#>     Fatigue        10.8    10.80       7.3  7.341

get_stats() returns the simulated statistics and get_rmse() the RMSEs between simulated and target statistics:

get_stats(result_vec)
#> $mean
#>    Apnea.1    Apnea.2 Depression    Fatigue 
#>   48.75073   17.34969   12.63333   10.80000 
#> 
#> $sd
#>    Apnea.1    Apnea.2 Depression    Fatigue 
#>  27.052032  20.051124  11.322644   7.341085
get_rmse(result_vec)
#> $rmse_mean
#> [1] 0.03875487
#> 
#> $rmse_sd
#> [1] 0.04150452

If SPRITE finds no distribution for an integer variable, the reason is stored per variable in error_msgs (NULL when SPRITE succeeded):

result_vec$error_msgs
#> [[1]]
#> NULL
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> NULL
#> 
#> [[3]]
#> NULL
#> 
#> [[4]]
#> NULL

1.5 Diagnostics

plot_convergence() shows the best objective value across iterations. For a stats2data_vec result, run selects the variable; Apnea.2 is the second variable. log_y = TRUE uses a logarithmic y axis, and the shaded band marks the region below thresh.

plot_convergence(result_vec, run = 2, log_y = TRUE)

The trajectory has 112 iterations. Integer variables are drawn by SPRITE without annealing, so their trajectory consists of a single value.

plot_cooling() shows the temperature schedule implied by init_temp, cooling_rate, and max_iter:

plot_cooling(result_vec)

1.6 Target vs. simulated statistics

plot_fit() plots the difference between simulated and target statistics. With standardised = FALSE, the differences are on the original scale; the shaded band marks +/- thresh. order = "fit" sorts the statistics by absolute difference.

plot_fit(result_vec, standardised = FALSE, order = "fit")

The same plots are available through plot(), with which selecting the panel:

plot(result_vec)                    # plot_convergence()
plot(result_vec, which = "cooling") # plot_cooling()
plot(result_vec, which = "fit")     # plot_fit()

1.7 Simulated data

The simulated data are stored in result_vec$data, one column per variable:

data_vec <- result_vec$data
head(data_vec)
#>    Apnea.1    Apnea.2 Depression Fatigue
#> 1 75.77349 18.2021350          8      14
#> 2 62.38032 11.3144337         19      20
#> 3 18.60938  2.7516503         15       7
#> 4 53.29988 26.4374525         16       9
#> 5 56.48064 40.9638859          5      21
#> 6 24.81849  0.1944602         25       6

data_long <- data.frame(
  variable = factor(rep(names(data_vec), each = nrow(data_vec)), levels = names(data_vec)),
  value    = unlist(data_vec, use.names = FALSE)
)
ggplot(data_long, aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 15, fill = "grey60", colour = "grey20") +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()

2. MLR module: Bardwell et al. (2007)

Bardwell et al. (2007) also report a multiple linear regression of Fatigue on the two apnea indices and Depression, with coefficients, standard errors, and the correlations of each predictor with Fatigue. optim_mlr() simulates data that reproduce these targets together with the marginal statistics from Section 1.

2.1 Encoding the targets 

reg_equation <- "Fatigue ~ Apnea.1 + Apnea.2 + Depression"
target_reg   <- c("(Intercept)" = 4.020, Apnea.1 = 0.023, Apnea.2 = 0.008, Depression = 0.438)
target_se    <- c(NA, 0.034, 0.048, 0.066)
target_cor   <- c(NA, NA, NA, 0.11, 0.20, 0.68)

target_reg and target_se follow the terms of reg_equation, intercept first. target_cor holds the upper triangle of the correlation matrix of all variables in target_mean, filled column by column in the order of target_mean: Apnea.1-Apnea.2, Apnea.1-Depression, Apnea.2-Depression, Apnea.1-Fatigue, Apnea.2-Fatigue, Depression-Fatigue. NA marks statistics that were not reported; they are excluded from the objective.

2.2 Running the optimizer

optim_mlr() first calls optim_vec() to simulate the marginals and then reorders the values of the predictors with simulated annealing, followed by hill climbing (hill_climbs). The objective is weight * correlation error + (1 - weight) * regression error, where the regression error includes the standard errors when target_se is given.

The call uses thresh = 0.001, sprite_prec = c(1, 1) as in Section 1, and the defaults otherwise (weight = 0.5, max_iter = 1e5, max_starts = 3, hill_climbs = 1e4; init_temp = NULL is calibrated from the objective changes of random swaps, cooling_rate = NULL is (max_iter - 10) / max_iter).

set.seed(2026)
result_mlr <- optim_mlr(
  N            = N,
  target_mean  = target_mean,
  target_sd    = target_sd,
  range        = range,
  integer      = integer,
  sprite_prec  = c(1, 1),
  reg_equation = reg_equation,
  target_cor   = target_cor,
  target_reg   = target_reg,
  target_se    = target_se,
  thresh       = 0.001
)

2.3 Inspecting the result 

result_mlr
#> stats2data MLR result
#>   N:          60 
#>   Equation:   Fatigue ~ Apnea.1 + Apnea.2 + Depression 
#>   Best objective: 0.00225996

The best objective value is 0.00226, which is not below thresh = 0.001.

summary(result_mlr)
#> stats2data MLR Summary
#> -----------------------------------------------
#> N: 60  | Model: Fatigue ~ Apnea.1 + Apnea.2 + Depression 
#> Best objective: 0.00225996 
#> 
#> RMSE
#>   Correlations:             0.00002284 
#>   Regression Coefficients:  0.0003972 
#>   Standard Errors:          0.006854 
#> 
#> Descriptives (Target vs. Simulated):
#>    variable target_mean sim_mean target_sd sim_sd
#>     Apnea.1        48.8    48.80      27.1 27.099
#>     Apnea.2        17.3    17.30      20.1 20.099
#>  Depression        12.6    12.60      11.3 11.283
#>     Fatigue        10.8    10.82       7.3  7.347
#> 
#> Coefficients (Target vs. Simulated):
#>         term target_reg  sim_reg target_se  sim_se
#>  (Intercept)      4.020 4.020297        NA 1.65638
#>      Apnea.1      0.023 0.023138     0.034 0.02754
#>      Apnea.2      0.008 0.008704     0.048 0.03809
#>   Depression      0.438 0.437831     0.066 0.06500
#> 
#> Correlations (Target vs. Simulated):
#>                pair target_cor sim_cor
#>     Apnea.1-Apnea.2         NA 0.28831
#>  Apnea.1-Depression         NA 0.02649
#>  Apnea.2-Depression         NA 0.22546
#>     Apnea.1-Fatigue       0.11 0.11001
#>     Apnea.2-Fatigue       0.20 0.20000
#>  Depression-Fatigue       0.68 0.67996

get_stats() returns the fitted lm object, the coefficients, standard errors, correlations (upper triangle in the order predictors, outcome), means, and SDs of the simulated data. coef() refits the regression and returns the coefficients:

stats_mlr <- get_stats(result_mlr)
names(stats_mlr)
#> [1] "model" "reg"   "se"    "cor"   "mean"  "sd"
summary(stats_mlr$model)
#> 
#> Call:
#> stats::lm(formula = frm, data = d)
#> 
#> Residuals:
#>      Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
#> -13.1641  -3.0217  -0.8974   4.5710  11.1889 
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>             Estimate Std. Error t value      Pr(>|t|)    
#> (Intercept) 4.020297   1.656380   2.427        0.0185 *  
#> Apnea.1     0.023138   0.027536   0.840        0.4043    
#> Apnea.2     0.008704   0.038093   0.228        0.8201    
#> Depression  0.437831   0.065002   6.736 0.00000000945 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> Residual standard error: 5.484 on 56 degrees of freedom
#> Multiple R-squared:  0.4713, Adjusted R-squared:  0.443 
#> F-statistic: 16.64 on 3 and 56 DF,  p-value: 0.0000000752
coef(result_mlr)
#> (Intercept)     Apnea.1     Apnea.2  Depression 
#> 4.020297185 0.023137936 0.008703818 0.437831483
get_rmse(result_mlr)
#> $rmse_cor
#> [1] 0.00002283587
#> 
#> $rmse_reg
#> [1] 0.00039721
#> 
#> $rmse_se
#> [1] 0.006854068

The marginal result of the internal optim_vec() call is stored in result_mlr$optim_vec and supports the methods of Section 1:

get_rmse(result_mlr$optim_vec)
#> $rmse_mean
#> [1] 0.008362809
#> 
#> $rmse_sd
#> [1] 0.02522139

2.4 Diagnostics

plot_convergence() shows the best objective value across the annealing iterations; first_iter skips leading iterations, here the first 10%:

n_iter_mlr <- length(result_mlr$track_objective)
plot_convergence(result_mlr, log_y = TRUE, first_iter = floor(n_iter_mlr / 10))

With ratio = TRUE, the plot shows the ratio of the correlation error to the regression error of the best candidate, with lines at its mean, median, and final value (show_mean, show_median, show_final). A ratio above 1 means that the correlation component is the larger of the two.

plot_convergence(result_mlr, ratio = TRUE)

The final ratio is 0.00509.

plot_cooling() uses the stored init_temp and cooling_rate, i.e. the values calibrated during the run:

result_mlr$inputs$init_temp
#> [1] 0.03931238
plot_cooling(result_mlr)

2.5 Balancing the objective with weight

weight sets how much the correlation and the regression components contribute to the objective. Objective values obtained with different weights are on different scales and are not compared directly; the unweighted RMSEs of get_rmse() are. The optimization is repeated with weight = 0.1:

set.seed(2026)
result_mlr_w01 <- optim_mlr(
  N            = N,
  target_mean  = target_mean,
  target_sd    = target_sd,
  range        = range,
  integer      = integer,
  sprite_prec  = c(1, 1),
  reg_equation = reg_equation,
  target_cor   = target_cor,
  target_reg   = target_reg,
  target_se    = target_se,
  thresh       = 0.001,
  weight       = 0.1
)
rbind(
  "weight = 0.5" = unlist(get_rmse(result_mlr)),
  "weight = 0.1" = unlist(get_rmse(result_mlr_w01))
)
#>                   rmse_cor     rmse_reg      rmse_se
#> weight = 0.5 0.00002283587 0.0003972100 0.0068540684
#> weight = 0.1 0.00194172165 0.0006876133 0.0009375174

The table shows how the RMSEs of the correlations, coefficients, and standard errors change with weight in this example. Which balance is preferable depends on which targets matter most for the intended use of the data. The remainder of this section continues with the weight = 0.5 result.

2.6 Target vs. simulated statistics 

plot_fit(result_mlr, standardised = FALSE)

With the default standardised = TRUE, the differences are divided by the target values (for targets of zero, the unstandardised difference is shown). The plot() method offers the same panels, including which = "ratio":

plot(result_mlr, which = "fit")
plot(result_mlr, which = "ratio")

2.7 Simulated data 

data_mlr <- result_mlr$data
head(data_mlr)
#>     Apnea.1   Apnea.2 Depression Fatigue
#> 1  64.13553 17.754307         11      18
#> 2  17.86473 15.232345         15      14
#> 3 110.29750 17.351951          0      15
#> 4  29.09759 32.718223         16      11
#> 5  47.35261 14.904594         11       7
#> 6  28.03631  1.847764          9       6
round(cor(data_mlr), 2)
#>            Apnea.1 Apnea.2 Depression Fatigue
#> Apnea.1       1.00    0.29       0.03    0.11
#> Apnea.2       0.29    1.00       0.23    0.20
#> Depression    0.03    0.23       1.00    0.68
#> Fatigue       0.11    0.20       0.68    1.00

3. ANOVA module: Reynolds and Besner (2008)

This section follows the empirical example of the accompanying manuscript. Reynolds and Besner (2008, Experiment 5) examined how contextual predictability affects response times in word and nonword naming; the study was among those replicated by the Open Science Collaboration (2015). To our knowledge, the raw data are not publicly available.

3.1 Reported summary statistics

The study reports a 2 x 2 within-subjects design (S = 16) with four cell means, indexed by stimulus type (Factor1) and switch condition (Factor2): 543, 536, 614, and 618 ms. It reports MSE = 3070 for the Factor1 effect, F(1, 15) = 30.5 (partial eta squared .670) for Factor1, and F < 1 for Factor2 (.002) and the interaction (.015).

The code of this section is the code of the empirical example in the manuscript, so it reproduces the results reported there.

S   <- 16
mse <- 3070
target_group_means <- c(543, 536, 614, 618)
eta2   <- c(0.002, 0.015)  # Factor2, Factor1:Factor2
df_err <- S - 1

The numerator mean squares implied by the cell means of the balanced 2 x 2 within-subjects design are:

m_cell  <- matrix(target_group_means, nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)  # rows: Factor1, cols: Factor2
m_grand <- mean(m_cell)
ms_f1   <- S * 2 * sum((rowMeans(m_cell) - m_grand)^2)
ms_f2   <- S * 2 * sum((colMeans(m_cell) - m_grand)^2)
ms_int  <- S * sum((m_cell - outer(rowMeans(m_cell), colMeans(m_cell), "+") + m_grand)^2)
c(ms_f1 = ms_f1, ms_f2 = ms_f2, ms_int = ms_int)
#>  ms_f1  ms_f2 ms_int 
#>  93636     36    484

The reported Factor1 statistics are consistent with each other: the implied mean square divided by the reported MSE gives F = 30.5, and F / (F + df_error) gives the reported partial eta squared of .670.

stopifnot(round(ms_f1 / mse, 1) == 30.5)
stopifnot(round(30.5 / (30.5 + df_err), 3) == 0.670)

For the two effects reported as F < 1, the F-statistics are set from the reported partial eta squared via F = eta^2 * df_error / (1 - eta^2) (one numerator degree of freedom). The modules require bounds for the outcome, which the study does not report; the range of the reported cell means is extended by four times sqrt(MSE), the residual SD implied by the MSE, and rounded outward. The summary statistics are encoded in one list of optim_aov() arguments:

F_value_derived <- c(round(ms_f1 / mse, 1), round(eta2 * df_err / (1 - eta2), 3))

sumstats <- list(
  S                  = S,
  levels             = c(2, 2),
  factor_type        = c("within", "within"),
  formula            = "outcome ~ Factor1 * Factor2 + Error(ID / (Factor1 * Factor2))",
  integer            = FALSE,
  target_f_list      = list(
    effect  = c("Factor1", "Factor2", "Factor1:Factor2"),
    F_value = F_value_derived
  ),
  target_group_means = target_group_means,
  range              = c(floor(min(target_group_means) - 4 * sqrt(mse)),
                         ceiling(max(target_group_means) + 4 * sqrt(mse)))
)
sumstats$target_f_list$F_value
#> [1] 30.500  0.030  0.228
sumstats$range
#> [1] 314 840

target_group_means lists the cells with Factor1 varying slowest (11, 12, 21, 22).

3.2 Simulating a dataset

optim_aov() is called with its default hyperparameters (max_iter = 3e4, thresh = 0.005, max_starts = 3, init_temp = 1e-3, cooling_rate = NULL, i.e. (max_iter - 10) / max_iter). The objective is the RMSE between the simulated and target F-statistics.

set.seed(2026)
result_aov <- do.call(optim_aov, sumstats)

3.3 Inspecting the output 

result_aov
#> stats2data ANOVA result
#>   Design:    2 x 2 (within, within)
#>   Subjects:   16 
#>   Effects:    Factor1, Factor2, Factor1:Factor2 
#>   Best objective: 0.00346117

The best objective value is 0.00346, which is below thresh = 0.005. The best objective value first fell below thresh at iteration 8493:

which(result_aov$track_objective < result_aov$inputs$thresh)[1]
#> [1] 8493
summary(result_aov)
#> stats2data ANOVA Summary
#> -----------------------------------------------
#> Design:     2 x 2 (within, within)
#> Subjects:   16 
#> Best objective: 0.00346117 
#> 
#> RMSE
#>   F-statistics: 0.003461 
#>   Group means:  0.0000000000009747 
#> 
#> -----------------------------------------------
#> F-values (Target vs. Simulated):
#>           effect target_F    sim_F
#>          Factor1   30.500 30.49911
#>          Factor2    0.030  0.02408
#>  Factor1:Factor2    0.228  0.22774
#> 
#> -----------------------------------------------
#> Group Means (Target vs. Simulated):
#>        cell target_mean sim_mean
#>  F1=1, F2=1         543      543
#>  F1=1, F2=2         536      536
#>  F1=2, F2=1         614      614
#>  F1=2, F2=2         618      618

The simulated F-statistics are 30.499, 0.024, 0.228 for Factor1, Factor2, and Factor1:Factor2 (targets 30.5, 0.030, 0.228); the F-statistic RMSE is 0.003 and the cell-mean RMSE 0.000000000000975.

Before the annealing, optim_aov() may shift the target cell means by less than thresh so that the means and F-statistics can be matched jointly. The values used are stored in adjusted_targets:

result_aov$adjusted_targets
#> $group_means
#> [1] 543 536 614 618
#> 
#> $F_values
#> [1] 30.500  0.030  0.228

get_stats() returns the ANOVA table of the simulated data (fitted with afex), the F-statistics, and the cell means; get_rmse() returns the two RMSEs:

get_stats(result_aov)
#> $model
#> Anova Table (Type 3 tests)
#> 
#> Response: outcome
#>                 num Df den Df    MSE       F     ges     Pr(>F)    
#> Factor1              1     15 3070.1 30.4991 0.43050 0.00005852 ***
#> Factor2              1     15 1495.2  0.0241 0.00029     0.8788    
#> Factor1:Factor2      1     15 2125.2  0.2277 0.00389     0.6401    
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> $F_value
#> [1] 30.49911423  0.02407665  0.22773815
#> 
#> $mean
#> 1_1 1_2 2_1 2_2 
#> 543 536 614 618
get_rmse(result_aov)
#> $rmse_F
#> [1] 0.003461175
#> 
#> $rmse_mean
#> [1] 0.0000000000009746616

3.4 Diagnostic plots

The two panels of the manuscript figure are obtained with (first_iter = 1 skips the first iteration):

plot_convergence(result_aov, first_iter = 1, log_y = TRUE)

plot_fit(result_aov, standardised = FALSE)

show_best = FALSE removes the marker of the best value and thresh = NULL the shaded band:

plot_convergence(result_aov, show_best = FALSE, thresh = NULL)

plot_cooling() shows the temperature schedule:

plot_cooling(result_aov)

3.5 Simulated data

The data are stored in long format, one row per subject and cell. The simulated observations lie within range; the second line checks whether any observation equals one of the bounds:

range(result_aov$data$outcome)
#> [1] 469.2889 735.7955
any(result_aov$data$outcome %in% sumstats$range)
#> [1] FALSE

data_aov <- result_aov$data
head(data_aov)
#>   ID Factor1 Factor2  outcome
#> 1  1       1       1 526.5609
#> 2  1       1       2 594.2713
#> 3  1       2       1 641.5214
#> 4  1       2       2 551.0167
#> 5  2       1       1 535.8782
#> 6  2       1       2 549.8449
aggregate(outcome ~ Factor1 + Factor2, data = data_aov, FUN = mean)
#>   Factor1 Factor2 outcome
#> 1       1       1     543
#> 2       2       1     614
#> 3       1       2     536
#> 4       2       2     618

ggplot(data_aov, aes(x = interaction(Factor1, Factor2, sep = "-"), y = outcome)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, colour = "grey40") +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = 4, size = 4) +
  labs(x = "Cell (Factor1-Factor2)", y = "Outcome") +
  theme_minimal()

Crosses mark the simulated cell means.

4. Parallel workflow: Reynolds and Besner (2008)

Each run of an optimizer is subject to randomness, and many datasets share the same summary statistics, so repeated runs return different datasets. parallel_optim() repeats the optimization with the same arguments and collects the runs. As in the manuscript, the ANOVA optimization is repeated 100 times on 6 parallel workers using future::multisession (Bengtsson, 2021); seed gives each run its own reproducible random-number stream.

result_parallel_aov <- parallel_optim(
  FUN   = optim_aov, # ANOVA module
  args  = sumstats,  # reported summary statistics
  runs  = 100,       # number of optimization runs
  cores = 6,         # number of parallel workers
  seed  = 2026,      # future.seed for parallel workers
  stop_conv = FALSE  # whether to stop once a run converges
)

cores = 1 (the default) runs the replications sequentially; cores > 1 requires the packages future and future.apply. Because every run has its own random-number stream derived from seed, the results do not depend on cores.

4.1 Inspecting the parallel output 

result_parallel_aov
#> stats2data parallel result
#>   Module: aov 
#>   Runs:   100 
#>   Best objective (across runs): 0.00106352 
#>   Mean objective (across runs): 0.0038539

100 of 100 runs have a best objective value below thresh = 0.005. Across runs, the best objective values range from 0.00106 to 0.00499, and the simulated observations of all runs range from 358.1 to 765.9:

max(sapply(result_parallel_aov$results, function(x) x$best_objective)) < .005
#> [1] TRUE
sum(vapply(result_parallel_aov$results,
           function(r) r$best_objective < r$inputs$thresh, logical(1)))
#> [1] 100
range(unlist(lapply(result_parallel_aov$results, function(r) r$data$outcome)))
#> [1] 358.1386 765.8632

summary() lists the best and mean objective values, the RMSE against the targets and between runs, and the target statistics aggregated across runs:

summary(result_parallel_aov)
#> stats2data Parallel Summary
#> -----------------------------------------------
#> Module: aov  | Runs: 100 
#> Best objective:  0.00106352 
#> Mean error:  0.0038539 
#> SD error:    0.00107989 
#> 
#> Target RMSE (across runs):
#>  metric     mean      sd      min      max
#>  rmse_F 0.003854 0.00108 0.001064 0.004993
#> 
#> Between-run RMSE:
#>  metric     mean       sd       min     max
#>  rmse_F 0.002037 0.001176 0.0003188 0.00747
#> 
#> Aggregated Statistics:
#>   F_value:
#>       mean   median       sd      min      max
#> 1 30.49988 30.50007 0.002090 30.49379 30.50390
#> 2  0.02439  0.02308 0.003290  0.02143  0.03728
#> 3  0.22786  0.22779 0.001234  0.22488  0.23112
#> 
#>   mean:
#>     mean median                 sd min max
#> 1_1  543    543 0.0000000000009403 543 543
#> 1_2  536    536 0.0000000000009664 536 536
#> 2_1  614    614 0.0000000000009346 614 614
#> 2_2  618    618 0.0000000000009585 618 618

get_stats() aggregates each statistic across runs (mean, median, SD, minimum, maximum):

get_stats(result_parallel_aov)
#> $F_value
#>          mean      median          sd         min         max
#> 1 30.49988225 30.50006753 0.002090449 30.49379382 30.50390112
#> 2  0.02439294  0.02307733 0.003290052  0.02143349  0.03727947
#> 3  0.22786082  0.22779020 0.001233544  0.22487923  0.23112459
#> 
#> $mean
#>     mean median                    sd min max
#> 1_1  543    543 0.0000000000009403361 543 543
#> 1_2  536    536 0.0000000000009663550 536 536
#> 2_1  614    614 0.0000000000009345567 614 614
#> 2_2  618    618 0.0000000000009584873 618 618

get_rmse() returns two RMSEs per run and metric: target_rmse, against the targets, and between_rmse, against the across-run mean of the simulated statistics. The per-run values are in raw:

par_rmse$target_rmse
#>   metric        mean          sd        min         max
#> 1 rmse_F 0.003853902 0.001079895 0.00106352 0.004992881
par_rmse$between_rmse
#>   metric        mean          sd          min         max
#> 1 rmse_F 0.002036642 0.001175672 0.0003187576 0.007469883

The mean F-statistic RMSE against the targets is 0.00385 (maximum 0.00499); the mean run-to-run RMSE is 0.00204. The run-to-run RMSE quantifies how much the simulated F-statistics vary between runs; it does not compare the runs with the original data.

4.2 Stability and fit across runs

The two panels of the manuscript figure are plot(), which draws plot_stability(), and plot_fit(). plot_stability() shows the distributions of both RMSEs across runs, faceted by metric:

plot_stability(result_parallel_aov)

plot_fit() shows the across-run mean difference per statistic, with error bars for the across-run range (error_type = "range", default) or mean +/- SD (error_type = "sd"); dots mark the individual runs.

plot_fit(
  result_parallel_aov,
  standardised = FALSE
)

plot_fit(result_parallel_aov, standardised = FALSE, error_type = "sd")

plot() draws plot_stability() by default (as in the manuscript script) and plot_fit() with which = "fit":

plot(result_parallel_aov)
plot(result_parallel_aov, which = "fit", standardised = FALSE)

4.3 Individual runs

The run with the lowest best objective value is stored in best; all runs are in results. Both are ordinary stats2data_aov objects and support the methods of Section 3:

result_parallel_aov$best
#> stats2data ANOVA result
#>   Design:    2 x 2 (within, within)
#>   Subjects:   16 
#>   Effects:    Factor1, Factor2, Factor1:Factor2 
#>   Best objective: 0.00106352
get_rmse(result_parallel_aov$best)
#> $rmse_F
#> [1] 0.00106352
#> 
#> $rmse_mean
#> [1] 0.0000000000009426415
head(result_parallel_aov$results[[2]]$data)
#>   ID Factor1 Factor2  outcome
#> 1  1       1       1 543.7920
#> 2  1       1       2 484.1879
#> 3  1       2       1 630.0790
#> 4  1       2       2 590.7470
#> 5  2       1       1 629.6518
#> 6  2       1       2 526.1276

4.4 Stopping at the first converged run

With stop_conv = TRUE, parallel_optim() stops launching runs once a run has converged. With cores > 1, runs are dispatched in batches of cores, so a whole batch completes before the check:

result_first_aov <- parallel_optim(
  FUN       = optim_aov,
  args      = sumstats,
  runs      = 12,
  cores     = 6,
  seed      = 2026,
  stop_conv = TRUE
)
result_first_aov
#> stats2data parallel result
#>   Module: aov 
#>   Runs:   6 of 12 (stopped early)
#>   Converged: TRUE (thresh = 0.005 )
#>   Best objective (across runs): 0.00317099 
#>   Mean objective (across runs): 0.00411833

6 of 12 requested runs were completed.
